### 5.1.4 Doctrinal Construction of Law & The Reconstruction of Individual Sovereignty: Toward Strict Liability & Enterprise Liability

Facing the structural failure of conventional doctrines of breach of contract and tort law, the global legal community is now compelled to radically reconstruct civil liability doctrines in alignment with the precautionary principle articulated by Hans Jonas (1979) within the ethics of modern technological responsibility. We must decisively abandon fault-based liability models when confronting damages inflicted by large-scale autonomous AI systems (Calo, 2014). Instead, civil law must pivot toward the implementation of **strict liability** and **enterprise liability** principles for developers and providers of large language models (Schwenzer et al., 2012). Just as the doctrine of product liability imposes liability upon manufacturers of electronic or pharmaceutical goods without requiring proof of malicious intent at the factory floor, AI providers must be held absolutely accountable for the psychological and financial harms suffered by users resulting from systemic failures or the manipulative designs of their products (Vandevelde, 2017).

Within this novel doctrinal framework, the burden of proof (*onus probandi*) must undergo a reverse burden of proof (Hogeveen, 2021). Victims or their heirs should no longer bear the impossible obligation of dismantling black-box algorithms to locate developer negligence. Conversely, once a factual causal relationship is established between intensive interaction with an AI system and the occurrence of severe psychological or financial harm—such as suicide, profound clinical depression, or deepfake-based financial fraud—the law must immediately presume the AI provider civilly liable, unless the corporation can establish *force majeure* or a pure error entirely outside the bounds of reasonable design control (subject to a rigorous state of the art defense) (Kotz, 2017). This approach harmonizes with the spirit of the EU AI Act 2024 (Regulation 2024/1689, particularly Article 5 concerning prohibited practices that manipulate human behavior and cause psychological harm) while reinforcing the mandate of the Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27/2022) in safeguarding the cognitive integrity of citizens from covert psychographic profiling exploitation.

This reconstruction is not merely a technical matter of material compensation, but a vital bulwark for individual sovereignty in the digital age, shielding human inner autonomy from algorithmic infiltration (Farahany, 2023). Human beings are not merely collections of data points whose emotions can be exploited to maximize the retention metrics of multinational corporations (Zuboff, 2019). By imposing strict liability upon AI providers, we transmit an uncompromising doctrinal message: technological innovation must never compromise human dignity and public mental health (Jonas, 1979). Civil law must transform from a passive referee in the circulation of commodities into an active guardian of the human cognitive ecosystem, ensuring that the boundaries of inner autonomy cannot be breached by the logic of the algorithmic market (Floridi, 2013). Only through this paradigm can our legal civilization survive the tempest of artificial intelligence, ensuring that technology remains an instrument to elevate human life rather than a silent labyrinth that destroys reason from within (Weizenbaum, 1976).
